tagline: Tree-lined parkways connect Minneapolis lakes, creek banks and the Mississippi riverfront.
intro: Grand Rounds follows tree-lined city parkways beside lakes, Minnehaha Creek and the Mississippi, with separate paths for walking and cycling. The Minneapolis Park and Recreation Board lists approximately 55 miles of parkways in seven segments. Designated a National Scenic Byway in April 1998, the system brings together the lakes, woodlands, wetlands and constructed waterways that the park board highlights in its account of the route. Explore Minnesota also points to a wildflower garden at Theodore Wirth Park and Lake Harriet’s rose garden along the drive.

In the 1880s, Minneapolis hired landscape architect Horace Cleveland to connect and preserve natural features through parks and parkways. His principal interest was the Mississippi gorge; later commissioners and superintendents extended the vision around the Chain of Lakes and along Minnehaha Creek. The intended ring remains incomplete: the park board identifies a missing link between the Mississippi and Northeast segments.

Begin on the western side, at Lake of the Isles in the Chain of Lakes. Continue toward Lake Harriet, then follow Minnehaha Creek east past Lakes Nokomis and Hiawatha to Minnehaha Falls. West River Parkway turns the journey north along the Mississippi gorge to the downtown milling district and Stone Arch Bridge. The western and northern parkways also reach Theodore Wirth Park, Victory Memorial Parkway and Northeast Minneapolis.

moments.title: Lake of the Isles
moments.text: Lake of the Isles has two wooded islands, but it once had four. Dredging in the 1880s reshaped a smaller lake and adjacent marsh; material removed from the water became parkland along the shore. Much of that fill was peat and silt, whose settling contributed to an unstable shoreline. The surviving islands, Mike’s Island and Raspberry Island, are protected wildlife refuges. Signs prohibit landing on either island. Paved walking and cycling paths trace the lake’s shore. Connected to Cedar Lake and Bde Maka Ska, Lake of the Isles has a long north arm bordered by the Kenwood, Lowry Hill and East Isles neighborhoods.
moments.notice: Two wooded islands remain within the reshaped lake.

moments.title: Minnehaha Falls
moments.text: Longfellow borrowed Minnehaha’s name for a character, not the other way round. His 1855 poem The Song of Hiawatha spread the falls’ fame, although he never visited them. Horace Cleveland designed the park as part of the Grand Rounds system. When the park board considered a photographic stand in the lower glen in 1889, Cleveland objected to putting the building near the falls. The creek drops 53 feet here, then continues through the lower glen toward the Mississippi. The lower glen also holds visible remains of a stone-and-earth mill dam built in 1853 or 1854.

moments.title: Stone Arch Bridge
moments.text: Stone Arch Bridge began as James J. Hill’s railway connection to a new Union Depot, completed across the Mississippi in 1883. Charles C. Smith designed its arches to accommodate Saint Anthony Falls and the surrounding terrain. The piers use Sauk Rapids granite; the upper structure uses limestone from Mankato and Iowa. Two arches were replaced by a truss during construction of the lock and dam in 1961–63. The last passenger train crossed in 1978. The Minnesota Department of Transportation took ownership in 1992, before the park board converted the bridge. In 1994 the bridge became a walking and cycling route.
